name: Temazepam (Restoril)
summary: Short-term benzodiazepine sleep medication for insomnia (trouble falling asleep or staying asleep). Works the same night, but can cause next-day grogginess and carries real dependence and withdrawal risk—especially with daily use.
description: Temazepam (Restoril) is a benzodiazepine used for short-term insomnia when safer options haven’t worked. It can help you fall asleep faster and stay asleep longer, usually the same night you take it. The tradeoff: next-day impairment, memory issues, sleep-walking–type behaviors in rare cases, and a high risk of physical dependence if used regularly. Never combine with alcohol or opioids—this can be fatal. Best used at the lowest effective dose, for the shortest time, and as-needed when possible.
patient_summary: Temazepam (Restoril) can help you fall asleep and stay asleep the same night you take it. It can also leave you groggy the next day and can be habit-forming with regular use. Never mix with alcohol or opioids—this combo can shut down breathing. Most people should use it short-term and only when safer insomnia treatments haven’t worked.

linked_conditions.context: FDA-labeled for short-term treatment of insomnia (trouble falling asleep and/or staying asleep). Typically reserved for situations where safer therapies (CBT-I, sleep hygiene, non-benzodiazepine options) aren’t working or aren’t available.

Temazepam is not an antidepressant or anti-anxiety first-line medication. If insomnia is being driven by anxiety, treating the underlying anxiety (therapy and/or a longer-term medication strategy) usually matters more than stacking nightly sedatives.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to temazepam or any component of the formulation
Myasthenia gravis (risk of worsening muscle weakness)
Sleep apnea syndrome (avoid due to respiratory suppression risk; listed as contraindicated in some countries)
Prior paradoxical reactions to alcohol and/or sedative medications (in some labeling)

efficacy_response.comparison_data: Generally better than no medication in the short term, but tolerance and dependence risk rise with ongoing use
efficacy_response.patient_text: Temazepam can help you fall asleep faster and stay asleep longer—often the same night. But it’s not a forever medication. With regular use, your brain can adapt (tolerance), and stopping suddenly can trigger rebound insomnia and withdrawal.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral absorption with hypnotic effect typically the same night
pharmacokinetics.onset: Same-night sedation; plan for a full night of sleep
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Classified as short-to-intermediate acting; next-day impairment risk increases with higher dose and shorter sleep time
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (mostly inactive metabolites; <3% as unchanged drug)

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Temazepam (Restoril) is a benzodiazepine sleep medication used for short-term insomnia—meaning trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. It’s usually reserved for when safer options (like CBT-I and non-benzodiazepine strategies) haven’t worked or aren’t accessible, because the dependence and next-day impairment risks are real.
items: {link:condition:insomnia:Insomnia (sleep maintenance)}: Waking up too early or waking up repeatedly
Short-term, high-impact insomnia: When poor sleep is causing safety or function problems and a short rescue strategy is needed

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: People describe temazepam in a pretty consistent way—quick sleepiness, less nighttime wake-ups, and then the tradeoffs. Here’s what that can feel like:

quotes: It hits like a heavy blanket—my brain finally shuts up.
I stopped doing the midnight doom-scroll thing and just fell asleep.
I didn’t feel “high,” I felt sleepy. Like my body got the message.
I still woke up once, but I actually got back to sleep.
I slept through the night for the first time in weeks.
Less tossing and turning, fewer wake-ups.
The sleep was real, but I felt foggy the next morning.
I woke up slow—like my brain was buffering.
I was functional, but not sharp.
items.note: Next-day impairment is more likely with higher doses, shorter sleep time, alcohol, or other sedatives.

items.category: Memory gaps & weird sleep stuff (rare but important)
quotes: I don’t fully remember going to bed.
I had a conversation and barely recall it the next day.
I did something at night and it felt like autopilot.
items.note: Benzodiazepines can cause anterograde amnesia and, rarely, complex sleep behaviors (like sleep-driving). If that happens, it’s a stop-and-call-your-prescriber situation.

quotes: It worked great at first, then I needed more to get the same effect.
When I skipped it, my sleep got worse than it was before.
I didn’t realize my body was depending on it until I tried to stop.
items.note: With ongoing use, the brain can adapt. That’s why temazepam is typically kept short-term and tapered if it’s been used regularly.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Temazepam is designed to work the night you take it. It reaches peak levels in about 1 to 2 hours, and it can still affect you the next day—especially if you don’t get a full night of sleep or if the dose is higher than you need.
key_points: Bedtime dosing: Take right before bed when you can dedicate a full night to sleep
1-2 hours: Peak effect for many people
Short-to-intermediate acting: Can help with sleep onset and sleep maintenance
Next-day impairment can happen: More likely with higher doses, older age, other sedatives, or shorter sleep duration
Half-life range: 3.5 to 18.4 hours (people vary a lot)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.value: Often improves sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance
sections.comparison: Better than no medication short-term, but not a long-term solution
sections.text: Temazepam can be effective for short-term insomnia—especially when you’re stuck in a cycle of not sleeping and your system is too revved to reset. Many people notice faster sleep onset, fewer awakenings, or both. The catch is that tolerance can build, and dependence risk increases with longer use and higher doses. That’s why it’s usually positioned as a short-term tool while the real insomnia treatment is happening (CBT-I, habit changes, treating anxiety/depression, adjusting stimulants, etc.).
sections.clinical_details: Benzodiazepine hypnotics can improve sleep in the short term, but they come with next-day impairment risk, paradoxical reactions in some patients, and a meaningful risk of dependence and withdrawal if used continuously. For many patients, the safest long-term plan is CBT-I plus targeted treatment of underlying drivers (anxiety, depression, trauma, circadian rhythm issues, substances, medical sleep disorders).

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Never combine temazepam with opioids or alcohol. This can shut down breathing and can be fatal.
sections.black_box: Concomitant use of benzodiazepines and opioids may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Reserve combined use for patients where alternatives are inadequate. Use the minimum effective dose and duration, and monitor closely for sedation and breathing problems.
other: Abuse, misuse, and addiction risk: Higher risk with substance use history or when combined with alcohol, opioids, or illicit substances
Physical dependence can develop with continued use; risk increases with longer duration and higher daily dose
Do not stop suddenly after regular use: Abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction can cause life-threatening withdrawal
Next-day impairment: Can impair driving, reaction time, and judgment the following day—especially with higher doses or short sleep time
Complex sleep behaviors (rare): Sleep-driving, sleep-eating, making calls while asleep—stop medication and seek urgent medical advice if this happens
Depression and suicidal risk: Avoid in depression when there’s concern about worsening mood or safety, except in acute/emergency situations
patient_counseling: Plan for a full night of sleep. If you can’t commit to adequate sleep time, skip it.
Zero alcohol. Don’t mix with opioids. Don’t stack with other sedatives unless your prescriber specifically tells you to.
If you feel unusually agitated, aggressive, disinhibited, or “not yourself,” stop and contact your prescriber.
If you do anything while “asleep” (driving, cooking, eating, phone calls) or have memory gaps, treat it as a serious adverse effect.
If you’ve been taking it regularly, don’t stop suddenly—taper with a plan.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: drowsiness, dizziness, next-day hangover, and mental fog. Less common but serious: paradoxical agitation, memory gaps, respiratory suppression (especially with opioids/alcohol), allergic reactions, and complex sleep behaviors.
plain_language_list: Memory gaps for things that happen after taking it (especially at higher doses)

common.patient_note: Sleepiness is the point, but it can spill into the next day. Higher doses, older age, and other sedatives make this worse.
This can raise fall risk—especially at night when you get up to use the bathroom. Move slowly and keep pathways clear.
Some people describe this as low energy or heaviness the next day.
Grogginess and reduced sharpness the next morning. If this happens, the dose is often too high or sleep time is too short.
This is part of why benzodiazepines can be misused. If you notice craving or using it for reasons other than sleep, tell your prescriber.
Not common, but it shows up in labeling.

serious: Respiratory depression (highest risk with opioids, alcohol, or significant respiratory disease): slow or shallow breathing, bluish lips, unresponsiveness. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe withdrawal with abrupt stop after continued use: agitation, tremor, sweating, nausea, vomiting, perceptual changes, delirium, and seizures. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Paradoxical reactions: agitation, aggression, disinhibition, hallucinations, worsening anxiety. Stop and contact your prescriber urgently.
Anterograde amnesia: memory gaps for events after dosing; can lead to risky decisions without recall.
Complex sleep behaviors: sleep-driving, sleep-eating, making calls while not fully awake. Discontinue and seek immediate medical advice.
Hypersensitivity reactions (rare but serious): anaphylaxis or angioedema. Emergency care; do not rechallenge.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Temazepam is a sedative. Most serious interactions are about stacking sedation—especially anything that slows breathing or knocks out your alertness.

items.risk: Profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death.
items.action: Avoid whenever possible. If there is no alternative, use the lowest dose for the shortest time and monitor closely for excessive sedation and breathing problems.

items.risk: Additive CNS depression with dangerous impairment, blackouts, falls, and potential respiratory suppression.
items.action: Absolute “no.” Don’t drink on nights you take temazepam, and don’t assume spacing it out makes it safe.

items.with: Other sedatives (sleep meds, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, muscle relaxants, sedating antihistamines like diphenhydramine, gabapentinoids, cannabis)
items.risk: Excess sedation, falls, confusion, memory impairment, and higher overdose risk.
items.action: Avoid stacking sedatives. If your prescriber intentionally combines, doses should be conservative and safety monitoring should be tighter.

items.with: Respiratory depressants and high-risk medical conditions (COPD, untreated sleep apnea)
items.risk: Increased risk of breathing suppression during sleep.
items.action: Dose reduction or avoidance is often appropriate. If sleep apnea is suspected, get evaluated—sedatives can make it worse.

items.risk: Temazepam is only a minor CYP3A4 substrate and primarily undergoes phase II metabolism, so interactions here are usually not the main story—but clinically meaningful interactions can still exist depending on the full medication list.
items.action: Medication list review matters. If you’re on multiple interacting drugs, your prescriber may reduce dose, adjust frequency, or choose a different option.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been taking temazepam regularly, don’t stop abruptly. Benzodiazepine withdrawal can be severe and, in some cases, life-threatening. A gradual taper lowers the risk of withdrawal symptoms and rebound insomnia.
key_points: Typical taper approach: Reduce by 7.5 mg every 1 to 2 weeks until the lowest available dose is reached, then stop
Go slower if: You’ve been on it long-term, you’ve had withdrawal before, you have high baseline anxiety, or prior taper attempts failed
Rebound insomnia: Temporary worsening of sleep can happen after stopping; it usually settles, but the first nights can be rough
Support that actually helps: CBT-I alongside tapering can improve success and reduce rebound insomnia
Red flags: Severe agitation, confusion, hallucinations, or seizure symptoms need urgent medical care

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Temazepam is taken at bedtime for short-term insomnia. Most adults start with a low dose and only increase if needed based on response and next-day effects.

adult.sleep_initial: 7.5 to 15 mg PO once nightly at bedtime, as needed
adult.sleep_titration: If needed, increase based on response and tolerability
adult.prn_use: Take only when you can commit to a full night of sleep; avoid routine nightly use when possible to reduce dependence risk
adult.elderly: Avoid when possible. If used: 7.5 mg PO at bedtime as needed (elderly/debilitated patients are more sensitive; higher fall and confusion risk).
adult.renal: No dosage adjustment necessary for kidney impairment; not significantly removed by hemodialysis/CRRT
adult.hepatic: No specific manufacturer dose adjustment provided; use caution and start low in hepatic impairment

sections.simple_explanation: Start low because next-day grogginess and falls are dose-related. If 7.5–15 mg helps you sleep without a morning hangover, that’s usually the sweet spot. If you need higher doses to get the same effect, that’s a sign your brain is building tolerance—and it’s time to reassess the plan.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Temazepam is generally avoided in pregnancy and used cautiously in breastfeeding. Older adults have a much higher risk of confusion, falls, and motor vehicle accidents, so most guidelines recommend avoiding benzodiazepines for insomnia in people 65+ unless there’s a compelling reason.
sections.pregnancy: In utero benzodiazepine exposure may cause fetal harm. While data are mixed and not perfectly definitive, late-pregnancy exposure can cause newborn sedation (hypotonia, lethargy, respiratory depression) and/or neonatal withdrawal (irritability, tremors, feeding difficulty, hyperreflexia). Nonpharmacologic therapy is preferred for insomnia during pregnancy when possible. If exposure occurs, newborn monitoring is recommended. Patients may be eligible for enrollment in the National Pregnancy Registry for Psychiatric Medications (866-961-2388).
sections.lactation: Temazepam is present in breast milk. Limited data suggest milk levels are often very low, but infant sedation and feeding problems have been reported with some benzodiazepines. If used while breastfeeding, monitor the infant for excessive sleepiness, poor feeding, respiratory depression, and inadequate weight gain. The decision should balance infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and the mother’s treatment needs.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid for insomnia in most adults age 65+ (Beers Criteria). Risks include impaired cognition, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle accidents. If a benzodiazepine is considered necessary for a different indication (not routine insomnia), dosing should be minimal and reassessed frequently.
sections.hepatic: Use caution and consider a lower dose and slower titration in hepatic impairment. Temazepam is often considered less impacted by liver dysfunction than some other benzodiazepines, but sedation and confusion risk still rise in medically complex patients.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment is typically required for kidney impairment. Temazepam is highly protein-bound and not meaningfully dialyzed; supplemental doses are not usually needed with dialysis modalities.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Respiratory status: Watch for shallow breathing, loud snoring, witnessed apneas, or unusual daytime sleepiness—especially with COPD, suspected sleep apnea, or any opioid exposure
Next-day impairment: Morning grogginess, slowed reaction time, driving risk, work/school performance impairment
Falls and balance: Nighttime unsteadiness, dizziness, near-falls; higher risk in older adults
Cognition and memory: Confusion, forgetfulness, amnesia for events after dosing
Mood and safety: Worsening depression, irritability, disinhibition, suicidal thinking—especially in patients with baseline mood disorders
Paradoxical reactions: New agitation, aggression, hallucinations, unusual behavior
Misuse risk: Early refills, dose escalation, using outside bedtime/sleep purpose, mixing with alcohol or other sedatives
Duration creep: If use is extending beyond short-term, reassess the diagnosis (sleep apnea, circadian issues, substance-related insomnia, anxiety/depression) and prioritize CBT-I

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Temazepam is available as oral capsules in multiple strengths, which helps with starting low and tapering down when needed.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Temazepam enhances the effect of GABA, the brain’s main calming neurotransmitter. Think of GABA like the nervous system’s brake pedal. By making GABA-A signaling stronger, temazepam decreases neuronal excitability, which can reduce arousal and make it easier to fall asleep and stay asleep.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Temazepam is not a first-line insomnia treatment. In psychiatry-world, the foundation is CBT-I and addressing what’s driving insomnia (anxiety, depression, trauma, stimulants, circadian rhythm mismatch, substances, medical sleep disorders like sleep apnea). Temazepam is typically a short-term “bridge” or rescue option when insomnia is severe and safer options haven’t worked. If you need it nightly to sleep, that’s usually a sign the plan needs an upgrade—not just a higher dose.

seo.title: Temazepam (Restoril): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects & Withdrawal
seo.description: Temazepam (Restoril) for insomnia: bedtime dosing (7.5–30 mg), how fast it works, next-day impairment, dependence risk, opioid/alcohol dangers, side effects, and how to taper safely.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Temazepam is used for short-term insomnia—trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. It’s typically reserved for situations where safer insomnia treatments (especially CBT-I) haven’t worked or aren’t available.

faqs.q: How long does temazepam take to work?
faqs.a: It’s designed to work the same night you take it. Many people feel sleepy within the first hour, with strongest effects around 1–2 hours after dosing.

faqs.q: What’s the usual temazepam dose for sleep?
faqs.a: Adults commonly start at 7.5–15 mg at bedtime as needed. If needed and tolerated, it can be increased up to 30 mg at bedtime. The goal is the lowest dose that helps you sleep without next-day impairment.

faqs.q: Can I take temazepam every night?
faqs.a: That’s usually not the plan. Temazepam is generally intended for short-term use because tolerance and dependence risk rise with ongoing nightly dosing. If you feel like you “need” it every night to sleep, it’s time to reassess the root cause of insomnia and shift toward CBT-I and other longer-term fixes.

It can be. Temazepam is a Schedule IV controlled substance. Regular use can lead to physical dependence, and misuse risk is higher when combined with alcohol, opioids, or other substances. If you notice cravings, dose escalation, or using it for reasons other than sleep, tell your prescriber early.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with temazepam?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol plus temazepam is a high-risk combination. It can cause dangerous sedation, blackouts, falls, and breathing suppression. If you drink that evening, skip temazepam.

faqs.q: Why is temazepam dangerous with opioids?
faqs.a: Both opioids and benzodiazepines can suppress breathing. Together, they can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. If you’re taking any opioid (even “as needed”), your prescriber should treat that as a major safety issue when considering temazepam.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Common effects include drowsiness, dizziness, lethargy, and a next-day “hangover” feeling. Some people get confusion or memory gaps, especially at higher doses or when combined with other sedatives.

faqs.q: Can temazepam cause sleepwalking or weird nighttime behavior?
faqs.a: Rarely, yes. Complex sleep behaviors like sleep-driving, cooking/eating, or making calls while not fully awake have been reported with sedative-hypnotics, including benzodiazepines. If anything like that happens, stop taking it and contact your prescriber urgently.

faqs.q: How do I taper off temazepam safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been taking it regularly, don’t stop suddenly. A common taper is reducing by 7.5 mg every 1–2 weeks until you reach the lowest dose, then stopping. People who’ve used it long-term often need a slower taper, and CBT-I during tapering can make a big difference.

faqs.q: Is temazepam safe for older adults?
faqs.a: Usually not. In people 65+, benzodiazepines increase the risk of confusion, delirium, falls, fractures, and car accidents. Most guidelines recommend avoiding temazepam for insomnia in older adults unless there’s a strong reason and safer options have failed.

faqs.q: Is temazepam safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: It’s generally avoided in pregnancy unless benefits clearly outweigh risks. Late-pregnancy benzodiazepine exposure can cause newborn sedation or withdrawal symptoms. Temazepam can pass into breast milk; if used while breastfeeding, infants should be monitored for sleepiness, feeding problems, breathing issues, and poor weight gain.
